accepted.reason: Observation-target alignment is strong (hospitalization rate mapped to H). Complexity is moderate (adds H) but still plausible. Main concern is identifiability of I->H and H outflow with only 31 training weeks in a single season; however, among the options it is the cleanest alignment without extra timing degrees of freedom.

Still aligns target to H, and a 1-week delay is plausible given surveillance semantics. However, adding an explicit delay on top of E->I and I->H timing increases non-identifiability risk in short single-season data; delay may trade off with transition rates and blur interpretability.

Target alignment remains good, but a fixed 2-week delay is more likely to over-shift peaks in a high-peak series and force compensatory parameter changes. With limited season length, this adds timing flexibility that is hard to identify and may destabilize peak/tail shape.

rejected.reason: Fractional memory is not well-justified here given short single-season data and already-added H compartment. Fractional order can overfit peakiness/tails and absorb delay/residence-time effects, worsening identifiability and interpretability without clear need.

suggested_edits.edit: Consider whether delayed_I (instead of H) should be the primary observation map for this short single-season series, given the stated weak identifiability of an explicit H compartment; if H is kept, avoid adding additional timing flexibility elsewhere.
If retained, treat the 1-week delay as optional and be cautious about redundancy with E->I and I->H timing; prefer keeping either the explicit delay or relying on transition times, not both.
If retained, justify the 2-week delay with strong prior surveillance knowledge; otherwise prefer 0–1 week to reduce peak-timing non-identifiability.
